sm: The mayor opened the November 10, 2026 work session and everyone was present. The first item, resolution 2026-88, asks to extend vesting rights for the Kurthers Glenn PUD, which has 45 single family lots, by one year to December 9, 2027. Staff said infrastructure is substantially complete, the final plat is not yet recorded, and the planning commission recommended approval eight to zero. The applicant said they expect to record the plat within days and are worried about timing for builders. Staff then introduced the Huffines Ridge rezoning and plan revision, which adds about four acres and 54 multifamily units, with one parking modification staff supports and a cross access modification it does not.

Goldberg Companies described a 54 unit for sale, twenty over twenty townhome style community, and a consultant explained that a vehicular connection to the Harper Apartments would need about 35,000 cubic yards of fill, so they propose a pedestrian connection instead. Alderman Burger welcomed for sale units and said he is not worried about connectivity. Alderman Potts asked about attainable housing, and the applicant said the units will be market rate, with parkland fees of about 5,400 dollars per home. The nearly finished Kurthers house will be conveyed to the parks department after inspection. Alderman Caesar confirmed the pedestrian path is shown on the plan.

Remaining answers on Huffines Ridge covered an emergency path to Arium and why there is no second pedestrian path, which is a ten foot retaining wall with rain gardens. An alderman thanked Goldberg for its work on the Kurthers house. The board moved to items four and five, a rezoning and plan revision for Iron Horse, an apartment complex at Franklin Road and Mack Hatcher. The applicant would replace two garage buildings with one building adding 30 units, for 300 total. Staff and the planning commission recommended disapproval, citing parking, including deferred parking, and two modifications of standards they oppose. A resident then spoke against the project over maintenance problems.

Several Iron Horse residents spoke in opposition. They raised parking, saying studies did not reflect near full buildings and that replacement spaces could be about 900 steps from a front door, as well as traffic at Franklin Road and Mack Hatcher and construction disruption near a preschool. One speaker, a retired civil engineer, said the intersection is already over capacity. Another, whose home faces the construction site, cited loss of garages, poor maintenance, and a shift from affordable to workforce housing. They asked the board to consider more than parking counts.

The final resident urged the board not to treat the decision as already settled. Snell Properties, the owner, said it is family owned, nearly 80 years old, and that 27 of the 30 new units are small one bedrooms of 670 square feet, renting for 200 to 300 dollars less than average. The consultant said only 11 of 16 garages are rented and seven other garages sit vacant. Parking counts on four days never exceeded 68 percent occupancy, and a recent early morning count showed about 60 percent. Color coded maps showed available spaces.

The consultant said even after the project there would be about 75 spare spaces on weekdays and 60 on weekends. Snell offered to relocate nearby residents with the same lease terms, restrict construction hours, lease 40 spaces from the Presbyterian church for workers, and reserve one parking space per apartment. Alderman Brown opposed it, saying the benefit does not justify reducing standards for market rate apartments. Alderman Blandon supported it, saying the developer has gone far to accommodate residents and the project uses existing infrastructure. The maintenance complaints, he said, are not part of this decision.

Alderman Potts said he first doubted the project but now sees it as a workable infill piece, and he stressed assigned parking. Alderman Burger said he was torn. He noted trees must be replaced, fire truck access must be preserved, and the new building is not wider but longer than the existing garages. He also said the owner has a business reason to remove empty garages and does not expect the 30 units to add meaningful traffic. The applicant confirmed each apartment will get a designated space near its building.

Alderman Burger added that residential traffic is sporadic and said he was still undecided. Alderman Peterson worried about parking on the entrance road. The consultant explained those parallel spaces would be deferred for two years and built only if a study shows they are needed, though they still count as code required. The vice mayor said the infrastructure is there, but she questioned the benefit of adding 30 units. Alderman Caesar asked about occupancy, and Snell said it has been 94 to 96 percent since 2020. He then asked about the parking layout shown in the slides.

After the parking layout was clarified, Alderman Caesar said he leans against the project, partly because of the failing grade on Franklin Road. Alderman Barnhill said the board should wait until it decides what to do about Franklin Road. He also asked how 30 to 35 affected units could be relocated at 94 to 96 percent occupancy. Snell said more than 100 apartments turn over each year, and the project is 13 to 15 months from starting. The mayor said he does not see it as smart infill. The board moved to item six, the comprehensive Franklin preservation plan, which appears on both agendas.

An alderman asked Julian Bib, who chaired the steering committee, to answer common questions. He said the city is not taking over preservation, that the plan is aspirational like the existing 2001 historic preservation plan and 2004 battlefield plan, and that nonprofits keep a role. He said retooling the Civil War Commission into a preservation commission was chosen after the committee considered an independent entity, an existing nonprofit, or city control. Reasons given were funding, possible rivalry among groups, public meetings and transparency, and the city's leading role. Committee members at that meeting voted unanimously for the retooling.

Details of the commission would come later, with zoning and ordinance changes. The group said the plan should be treated like other plans rather than picking out parts, and one member called it the city's best comprehensive plan. One alderman worried that pages naming areas like Royal Oak and Rebel Meadows are not truly historic. Julian replied that these are study areas, not historic overlays, and any overlay would need board approval and owner engagement. Another alderman hoped for strong leadership that could unite the divided preservation community, and said he likes the legacy neighborhoods being included because starter homes are being torn down.

Aldermen discussed other cities requiring replacement homes to match a neighborhood's style, and one asked how the commission would coordinate with departments and the planning and historic zoning commissions. The board then moved quickly through item seven, a change order of 285,743 dollars and 66 cents on the East McEwen Drive phase four contract, with no questions. Item eight covered options for widening Franklin Road from Mack Hatcher Parkway to Mallory Station. A three lane option costs about 14 million dollars, needs 10 acquisitions, and has no sidewalks. A three lane enhanced option costs about 22 million, needs 22 tracts, and would start around 2033. A five lane option needs about 25 tracts and would start around 2035.

Staff said the project is not in the state's ten year plan, federal funding is unlikely, and all options need major electrical relocation. They asked for guidance and offered to model other alternatives. Alderman Brown said to do it right the first time, use developer funds from nearby projects, and start right of way acquisition now. Staff agreed to meet on acquisition but said engineering must come first. Another alderman wanted five lanes extended to Gateway Village. The vice mayor questioned spending about 30 million dollars of city money and whether Legends Club Lane is the real bottleneck, and noted staff had looked at filling small gaps.

An alderman said Hillsboro Road in front of Franklin High cost about 25 million, was paid entirely by Franklin taxpayers, and took 20 years. They argued the board should plan for ten years out, and another said the state will not help until its funding model changes. Next came the fire department schedule analysis. Eric introduced it as weighing service, impact on the team, and cost. Sky Ghart of budget and performance said the update adds peer city data on unit responses versus call volume and the share of general fund spent on public safety.

Sky Ghart said the peer comparison covers 10 cities, and a regional pay comparison covers 11 cities, with notes that some offer different medical services. Franklin starts firefighters at 57,200 dollars and laterals at 60,632, with a 5,000 dollar emergency medical technician stipend and a paramedic stipend rising to 15,000 dollars. About 79 percent of on shift staff hold one of those certifications. Other cities' entry salaries range from 37,519 to 62,714 dollars. Staff said Franklin is strongest on paramedic pay and will look at pay in the coming budget. In April 2026 there were 545 completed applications, and 225 took the written exam.

Of the 108 who attended in person testing, 80 were placed on the certification list and 14 were hired. In person attendance has risen each year. In 2025 the department had 14 departures, eight of them retirements, for 8 percent turnover, or 3 percent excluding retirements. Through August 2026 there were 16 departures, 12 retirements, for 9 percent, or 2 percent excluding retirements. Retirees averaged about 26 and a half years of service. Captain Jay Gamble said a 24 on 48 off schedule means 728 more hours per year than a 40 hour week, about ten and a half years over a 30 year career, and discussed sleep, cancer exposure, mental health and work life balance.

Staff said they are consulting health clinicians, still refining the cost estimates, and will bring them back in coming months, with possible savings and funding sources. They will meet with Williamson County and Brentwood about emergency medical transport and service expectations. David Edge, a 23 year firefighter, thanked the board and said this is about health and safety. Tim Engel, whose son is a firefighter, urged Franklin to lead on this. Alderman Brown said the question is how to decide, since taxpayer money is involved.

Alderman Brown asked for a side by side of current and future state covering minimum staffing, training, benefits, equipment, overtime and transition costs. He asked staff to narrow the peer cities to those that changed schedules and report effects on operations, cost, recruiting, retention and health. Another alderman noted that Franklin leads and asked about the gap between estimated and department costs. A question on Brentwood and Germantown hours was answered as payroll treatment of sleeping time under federal wage rules. Alderman Caesar said there may be an option C, and Alderman Fox urged trust but verify with peer groups.

Alderman Fox said he wants to understand why carcinogen exposure differs across shifts. The mayor said item ten is deferred until December. Max presented the sidewalk gap project on the GoVocal platform, with changes after the last meeting. The city starts at 50 50 cost sharing with neighborhoods and HOAs, major roads are handled through capital projects, and the system allows idea submissions, status tags and a default response email. Alderman Brown apologized for his earlier reaction and praised the work. Alderman Caesar said residents want clarity on sidewalks, multi use paths and bike paths after the ebike rules, and staff is preparing a map. The session then ended with a ten minute break.
